name: Treaty with the Quinaielt, etc., 1855 (Treaty of Olympia)
promises: Article 2: a tract or tracts sufficient for the tribes' wants, to be selected by the President and set apart for their exclusive use, closed to white residents without permission.
Article 3 secured the right of taking fish at all usual and accustomed grounds and stations in common with all citizens, with hunting, gathering and pasturing on open and unclaimed lands.
Article 4: $25,000, paid in yearly instalments that began at $2,500 and fell to $1,000.
Article 10: an agricultural and industrial school, mechanics, a physician and medicine for twenty years.

breaches.what: In the case the United States brought in 1970, which names the Treaty of Olympia and the Quinault, Quileute and Hoh, the Supreme Court upheld the ruling that the treaty fishing clause secures the tribes a share of the fish, and recorded that the State Game Department refused to comply with the federal decree and that state courts barred the Fisheries Department from complying.

landTaken: The cession described in Article 1, on the Washington coast between the Makah and Chinook lands.
compensation: $205,172.40 to the Quinault and Queets by compromise (ICC Docket 242, 1962). The Quileute and Hoh claim (Docket 155) was also settled; its amount was not recorded in this pass.
today: The treaty fishing right is enforced under the continuing jurisdiction of United States v. Washington.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history says that under the Treaty of Olympia the Quileute were to give up their lands and move to Taholah, that they reserved hunting, fishing and gathering rights at their usual and accustomed places and were promised health care, education and job training in exchange for over 800,000 acres, and that a one-square-mile reservation was set up for them at La Push in 1889, the year a settler burned all 26 houses there.
The Tribe publishes the text of the Treaty of Olympia on its natural resources pages, where its fisheries and resource work is grounded.
The Tribe says it protects and enhances its natural resources by exercising its Treaty Rights, and that its 443-acre reservation at the mouth of the Hoh River was set up by Executive Order in 1893.

openQuestions: Timber mismanagement on Quinault allotments (United States v. Mitchell, 1980 and 1983) concerns trust duties under statutes rather than this treaty and was not recorded as a breach.
The Quinault Indian Nation's own account of the treaty was not found on its website in this pass.
The list of tribes in the culvert proceeding was not confirmed from the Ninth Circuit opinion, which could not be opened.
Audit 2026-11-08: Kappler dates the treaty July 1, 1855 and January 25, 1856 (signed at the Qui-nai-elt River, then at Olympia); signed is kept as July 1, 1855.
Audit 2026-11-08: the Article 4 promise reworded to the instalments the article states; "over twenty years" was a sum of the schedule, not a figure in the text.
